comparison: Perfect agreement on the paradoxical finding (C68-C70) that PGS accuracy differs across covariates but interaction terms don't improve prediction. Both evaluations find this result well-supported and methodologically important.

Complete agreement on quantile regression findings (C7-C8, C78-C87). Both evaluations explicitly highlight this as an important and well-supported methodological contribution for understanding PGS performance differences across strata.

Strong agreement on correlation findings (C5, C71-C77). Both evaluations support the finding that covariates with larger main effects and interaction effects stratify individuals by PGS performance. OpenEval also includes C6 which is not explicitly mentioned in peer review.

Strong agreement on interaction effect findings (C4, C55-C67). Both evaluations support the identification of covariates with significant interaction effects. OpenEval includes additional methodological claims (C53-C54, C141-C144) about PGS correction that peer review doesn't explicitly address.

Both support the main finding of differential PGS predictive power across covariates (C2-C3, C33-C38, C44). OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and replication, while peer review describes results as 'interesting and well-supported.' OpenEval includes additional claims (C39, C138-C140) not explicitly mentioned by peer reviewers.

Agreement on machine learning/nonlinear model findings (C9, C88-C94). Both evaluations support that nonlinear models provide substantial performance gains. OpenEval includes additional methodological details (C145-C151) about validation procedures not explicitly discussed in peer review.

Agreement on the GxAge approach for improving PGS performance (C10, C95-C99). Both evaluations support this methodological contribution. OpenEval includes additional technical claims (C152-C160) about implementation details not explicitly addressed by peer reviewers.

Both address ancestry-specific differences (C47-C48). However, OpenEval rates this as UNCERTAIN due to insufficient sample sizes and need for validation, while peer review accepts it as part of the convincing analysis. OpenEval also includes C46 which explicitly notes the need for larger samples.

Both address study design and methodology (C28-C31). OpenEval provides comprehensive evaluation of all methodological details (C1, C118-C135), while peer review focuses on accepting the multi-cohort, multi-ancestry design as appropriate without detailed critique.

OpenEval identifies negative/null findings (C41-C43, C45, C65-C67) regarding failure to replicate some previously reported associations. These specific null results are not explicitly discussed in peer review comments.

OpenEval supports findings about age-related heritability changes (C49-C52) and why age-matching GWAS doesn't eliminate age effects. These specific claims are not explicitly addressed in peer review comments.

OpenEval rates clinical implications and mechanistic speculations (C100-C105) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are explicitly speculative and require validation. Peer review does not specifically address these interpretative claims.
OpenEval supports the study's acknowledgment of limitations and future directions (C106-C110). These specific limitation and future work claims are not explicitly discussed in peer review comments.

OpenEval rates mechanistic explanations for observed patterns (C111-C114) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculative hypotheses lacking direct empirical support. Peer review does not specifically evaluate these mechanistic claims.
OpenEval supports the literature context and background claims (C11-C27) as accurately representing the field. Peer review does not explicitly evaluate these background/contextual claims.

OpenEval supports the summary statements about study contributions (C115-C117), though notes some findings require further validation. Peer review does not explicitly address these concluding summary claims.
